passage: At morning assembly, the principal asked the whole school to stand in silence for one minute for the families hit by the floods. Charu stood still for a few seconds, then started swinging her arms and humming. A few children giggled. Pradeep Sir, standing behind the KG line, bent down and quietly took her hand. He pressed one finger into her palm, then another, counting slowly. Charu watched his fingers and stopped humming. When the minute ended, she whispered, “That was long.” “It was. You managed it.”

qa.q: Why did the school stand in silence?
qa.a: For the families hit by the floods.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she started swinging her arms and humming?
qa.a: She was probably restless and finding the long silence hard, not being disrespectful.

qa.q: How did Pradeep Sir help Charu stay quiet?
qa.a: He quietly held her hand and counted with his fingers in her palm, giving her something calm to focus on.

qa.q: How might the other children see Charu's humming?
qa.a: Some found it funny and giggled, which could make it harder for everyone to stay quiet.

grounding: A preschooler finds a minute of collective silence hard, and her teacher gives gentle help to keep the hush.

passage: I'm Lavanya, Aditi's big sister. At Dada's remembrance prayer, everyone sat on the floor with their eyes closed for a long silence. Aditi, who's four, wriggled and whispered, “Is it finished?” Mummy didn't shush her crossly. She held Aditi's hand and squeezed it gently, once for each breath. Aditi squeezed back. They kept doing it. I don't know if Aditi understood why we were quiet, but she stayed still till the end, leaning on Mummy's arm.

qa.q: What did Aditi whisper during the silence?
qa.a: “Is it finished?”

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling as she wriggled?
qa.a: She was probably restless and bored in the long silence, and unsure how long it would last.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Aditi stay quiet?
qa.a: She held her hand and squeezed once for each breath, a quiet game that helped Aditi hold still.

qa.q: How did Lavanya see Aditi's stillness at the end?
qa.a: Lavanya wasn't sure Aditi understood why they were quiet, but noticed she stayed still, leaning on Mummy.

grounding: A sister observes a preschooler find a long prayer silence hard, and their mother helps with a quiet hand-squeeze game.

passage:
Monday: At nap time in the playschool, Parveen chatted to the girl on the next mat until Nilesh Sir had to move her.
Wednesday: Nilesh gave Parveen a soft toy tortoise. “Tortoise is sleepy. Can you breathe slowly with him?” She held it on her tummy and watched it go up and down. She whispered to it only twice.
Friday: Parveen took the tortoise from the basket herself, lay on her mat and breathed. The room was silent. After a while, Nilesh saw her eyes had closed.

qa.q: What soft toy did Nilesh Sir give Parveen?
qa.a: A tortoise.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling at nap time on Monday?
qa.a: She was probably wide awake and restless, finding the quiet hard, so she chatted instead.

qa.q: What small step helped Parveen keep the hush?
qa.a: Giving her the tortoise to breathe slowly with gave her a calm focus during the long quiet.

qa.q: How might the girl on the next mat feel by Friday?
qa.a: She'd likely be glad of the quiet, able to rest without chatter.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler learns to stay quiet at nap time with gentle help from her teacher.

passage:
“Sangeeta Aunty, why are you going round and round with the lamp?”
Asif stood at the neighbours' door during Diwali, watching the aarti.
Sangeeta smiled. “In our family, we move the lamp in circles to say thank you and show love to God. The light means goodness.”
“Can I watch?”
“Of course.”
The bell rang, and everyone sang. Asif stood very still.
Afterwards he said, “At Eid we light lamps too, on the balcony.”
“Light is special for lots of families,” said Sangeeta, and gave him a laddoo.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta's family move the lamp in circles?
qa.a: To say thank you and show love to God.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as he watched the aarti?
qa.a: He was curious and respectful, standing very still, and then felt connected when he remembered his own family's lamps.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta help the ritual mean more to Asif?
qa.a: She explained simply why her family does it, so he understood more than just the actions.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when Asif mentions Eid lamps?
qa.a: She likely feels warm and pleased that he saw something shared between their families.

grounding: A child watches a neighbour's aarti and learns why the ritual matters, connecting it to his own family's festival.

passage:
Note by Saurabh, KG teacher.
Today was Siddharth's birthday. When we sang and he blew out the candles, he asked, “Why do we blow them?” I said, “In many families, it's a way to mark that you're one year older and to make a wish.” He thought, then asked if he could blow them again for his friend's birthday next week. I told him the candles belong to the birthday child, but he could sing loudest. He practised singing all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Siddharth ask if he could do next week?
qa.a: Blow the candles again for his friend's birthday.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he asked why they blow the candles?
qa.a: He was curious about the ritual, wanting to understand it, not just copy it.

qa.q: How did Saurabh help the ritual's meaning grow?
qa.a: Saurabh explained simply that it marks being a year older and making a wish, and that the candles belong to the birthday child.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's friend feel next week?
qa.a: The friend would likely feel special, blowing the candles while Siddharth sings loudest.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler asking why birthday candles are blown and learning the meaning behind the ritual.

passage: At the first harvest, Omkar Dada carried the first bundle of wheat to the edge of the field and placed it under the neem tree with a lamp. Ira watched, holding her mother's hand. “Why are you giving wheat to the tree, Dada?” He knelt. “It's our way of saying thank you, to the earth and the rain, before we eat.” Ira thought. “Like saying thank you for food?” “Exactly.” Ira picked up a single grain and put it next to the bundle. “My thank you.”

qa.q: Where did Dada place the first bundle of wheat?
qa.a: Under the neem tree, with a lamp.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she added her own grain?
qa.a: She felt proud and included, wanting to give her own thank you after understanding the ritual.

qa.q: What did Dada do that helped the ritual mean more than imitation?
qa.a: He explained simply that it was a way of saying thank you to the earth and rain, linking it to something Ira knew.

qa.q: How might Dada feel when Ira adds her grain?
qa.a: He likely feels moved and happy that she understood and joined in.

grounding: A child watches a harvest ritual and learns from her grandfather why it matters, adding her own thank you.

passage: Every evening in Stockholm, when Oskar came home from work, Kofi met him at the door with a drawing covered in red hearts. “I love you, Papa. This many.” He'd point at every heart. On Saturdays he gave Oskar the last piece of his favourite licorice, even though he loved it. One night Kofi said, “I love you more than the whole sky and all the fish.” Oskar laughed. “That's a lot.” “It's everything,” Kofi said, and fell asleep on his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Kofi give Oskar on Saturdays?
qa.a: The last piece of his favourite licorice.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he said he loved Oskar more than the sky?
qa.a: He felt deep affection and wanted to show it in the biggest words he knew, though his words ran ahead of his understanding.

qa.q: What small acts show Kofi's love?
qa.a: Giving drawings with hearts every evening and sharing his favourite sweet show love through repeated small acts.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel each evening at the door?
qa.a: He likely feels loved and warm, looking forward to Kofi's hearts.

grounding: A preschooler shows love through repeated drawings of hearts, sharing a favourite sweet and big words.

passage: In the hospital waiting room, Gurpreet sat with Disha, the nurse on duty, while her mother had a check-up. She drew a big pink heart, then another, then another, until the page was full. “For Mummy. So she gets better fast.” Disha smiled. “She'll love it.” When her mother came out, Gurpreet ran and pressed the drawing into her hands. “I love you this many!” Her mother knelt and hugged her. “And I love you this many,” she said, and kissed each heart.

qa.q: What colour hearts did Gurpreet draw?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as she filled the page with hearts?
qa.a: She felt loving and a bit worried about her mother's check-up, showing care the way she knew how.

qa.q: What did Disha do that supported Gurpreet?
qa.a: Disha stayed with Gurpreet, smiled and assured her that her mother would love the drawing.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother feel when she receives the drawing?
qa.a: She'd feel touched and deeply loved, which is why she kisses each heart.

grounding: A preschooler draws hearts for her mother at the hospital, showing love through a small act.

passage: I'm Ujjwal, Irawati's big brother. Irawati says “I love you” to everyone: Mummy, Papa, the milkman, even the stray cat. At first I thought she didn't mean it. But every evening she saves half her sweet for Dadi and takes it to her room. Every morning she gives her doll a kiss before school. I don't know if she knows what love really means yet, but she does something kind every single day.

qa.q: What does Irawati save for Dadi every evening?
qa.a: Half her sweet.

qa.q: What might Irawati be feeling when she says “I love you” to everyone?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and affectionate, and her words may run ahead of full understanding. Ujjwal isn't sure what she understands.

qa.q: What shows Irawati's love more than her words?
qa.a: Her small daily acts, like saving half her sweet for Dadi and kissing her doll.

qa.q: How has Ujjwal's view of Irawati's love changed?
qa.a: He first thought she didn't mean it, but now notices her daily kindnesses.

grounding: A brother observes a preschooler's love shown through repeated small acts more than through her many I love yous.

passage: In the flat in Cairo, the baby, Dalia, was asleep in her basket. Jamal tiptoed over and knelt beside it. He stroked her head very softly with two fingers, the way his mother did. “Shh, habibti,” he whispered, in a tiny voice. He tucked her blanket higher, then sat back on his heels and watched her breathe. His mother, in the doorway, didn't say anything. She just smiled. Jamal whispered without looking up, “She's so small.”

qa.q: What did Jamal tuck higher?
qa.a: Dalia's blanket.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling as he stroked Dalia's head?
qa.a: He felt tender and protective of his tiny sister, shown in his gentle touch and quiet voice.

qa.q: Where did Jamal learn this gentle way of caring?
qa.a: From watching his mother, who strokes the baby's head the same way.

qa.q: How might Jamal's mother feel watching him from the doorway?
qa.a: She likely feels moved and proud, seeing him copy the care he has been given.

grounding: A preschooler strokes his baby sister's head with soft protective care, learned from how his mother cares for them.

passage: At the preschool's quiet corner, Tenzin tucked the toy rabbit into a shoebox bed. He folded a hanky over it and patted it three times. “Goodnight, Rabbit. I'm right here,” he whispered. Salma Ma'am, nearby, asked softly, “Where did you learn to tuck in so nicely?” “My Papa does it for me,” said Tenzin. “Three pats.” He put a finger to his lips when another child came close. “Shh. Rabbit's sleeping.” The other child whispered too.

qa.q: How many times did Tenzin pat the rabbit?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as he tucked the rabbit in?
qa.a: He felt tender and caring toward the rabbit, gentle like his father is with him.

qa.q: What does this scene show about where tenderness comes from?
qa.a: It is learned through being cared for; Tenzin copies his Papa's three pats.

qa.q: How might the other child see Tenzin's care for the rabbit?
qa.a: That child picked up the gentle mood and whispered too, respecting the pretend sleep.

grounding: A preschooler tucks a toy into bed with gentle touch and quiet voice, copying the tenderness he receives from his father.

passage: I'm Madhav, from the next building. On Sunday, a puppy with a hurt leg was lying by our gate. Salma, who is five, knelt a little way away and held out her hand slowly. When the puppy sniffed it, she stroked its ear with one finger and whispered, “Poor baby. It's okay.” She didn't pick it up. Her mother brought water and phoned the animal shelter. Salma stayed near, speaking softly the whole time. I don't know where she learned to be so gentle.

qa.q: Who did Salma's mother phone?
qa.a: The animal shelter.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as she stroked the puppy's ear?
qa.a: She felt tender and worried for the hurt puppy, shown by her gentle touch and soft voice.

qa.q: What did Salma's mother do that kept things safe?
qa.a: She brought water and phoned the animal shelter, so the puppy got help without Salma picking it up.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Salma's gentleness?
qa.a: Madhav is struck by it and wonders where she learned to be so gentle.

grounding: A neighbour observes a preschooler showing tender care to a hurt puppy with a gentle touch and quiet voice.

passage:
Note by Irawati, nursery teacher, Monday.
A new girl joined today and stood by the door holding her mother's dupatta. Before I could go over, Parveen walked up, waved, and said, “Hello! I'm Parveen. You can sit next to me.” She patted the mat and offered her the blue crayons, her favourites. The new girl sat down. I had modelled saying hello to every new child at the door, and it seems Parveen was watching. By snack time, the two of them were sharing a paratha.

qa.q: What colour crayons did Parveen offer?
qa.a: The blue crayons, her favourites.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when she walked up to the new girl?
qa.a: She seemed friendly and confident, eager to include the new girl, and perhaps proud to copy her teacher.

qa.q: What helped Parveen know how to welcome a newcomer?
qa.a: Irawati had modelled saying hello to every new child at the door, and Parveen copied it.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel when Parveen offers her a seat?
qa.a: She'd likely feel relieved and included after standing shyly by the door.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler welcoming a new child with a hello, a seat and her favourite crayons, copying what the teacher modelled.

passage: Relatives were coming from the next village, and Varun swept the courtyard. When the cart stopped at the gate, Varun folded his hands. “Namaste, Mausaji! Come, come.” Lalit copied him, hands folded, and then ran to drag a chair over the bumpy ground. “Sit here! It's the best chair!” He waved at the cousins too, jumping. The cousins, shy, hung back. Lalit took the youngest one's hand. “Come see our calf.” Varun smiled. The cousins followed Lalit to the shed.

qa.q: What did Lalit want to show the youngest cousin?
qa.a: Their calf.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling as he dragged the chair over?
qa.a: He felt excited and eager to make the guests feel welcome, proud to offer the best chair.

qa.q: How did Varun's greeting help Lalit welcome the guests?
qa.a: By folding his hands and inviting them in, Varun modelled a warm welcome that Lalit copied.

qa.q: How might the shy cousins feel when Lalit takes one of them by the hand?
qa.a: They'd likely feel less shy and more included, which is why they followed him to the shed.

grounding: A preschooler copies his father's welcome, offering a chair and inviting a shy cousin to play.

passage: At the kindergarten in Nairobi, a new girl, Nour, stood by the gate holding her father's hand tight. Wanjiru ran over. “Karibu! That means welcome.” She waved both hands. Nour didn't answer. Wanjiru pointed at the sandpit. “Do you want to play?” Nour looked at her father, then nodded. Wanjiru held out her hand. Nour let go of her father and took it. Their teacher, watching, said “Welcome, Nour” at the door, too. By lunchtime, Nour was saying “Karibu” to the next new boy.

qa.q: What does “Karibu” mean?
qa.a: Welcome.

qa.q: What was Nour feeling as she held her father's hand tight?
qa.a: She was probably shy and nervous in a new place, unsure whether to join in.

qa.q: What made Wanjiru's welcome work?
qa.a: She greeted warmly, explained the word and offered a clear invitation to play, holding out her hand.

qa.q: How might the next new boy feel when Nour says “Karibu” to him?
qa.a: He'd likely feel welcomed and less alone, as Nour did that morning.

grounding: A preschooler welcomes a new child with a greeting and an invitation to play, teaching inclusion.

passage: The zoo trip was planned for Sunday, and Vijay had packed his binoculars on Saturday night. On Sunday morning, it poured. Tanuja said, “Sorry, beta, the zoo is cancelled today.” Vijay dropped onto the sofa, shoulders slumped, lower lip out. “It's not fair. I wanted to see the tiger.” Tanuja sat beside him. “You're really disappointed. You were so excited.” He nodded, eyes wet. She didn't rush to fix it. After a while he sighed, picked up the binoculars, and started spying on the pigeons.

qa.q: What had Vijay packed on Saturday night?
qa.a: His binoculars.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he dropped onto the sofa?
qa.a: He was disappointed and let down that the zoo trip was cancelled, especially after being so excited.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that helped Vijay get through the letdown?
qa.a: She named his disappointment and let it pass without rushing to fix it.

qa.q: What would change if Tanuja had said “Stop sulking, it's only a zoo”?
qa.a: Vijay might feel dismissed and stay upset longer, instead of recovering by himself.

grounding: A preschooler sulks when a zoo trip is cancelled, and his mother names the disappointment and lets it pass.

passage:
“Papa, I didn't win.”
Ritu came out of the school hall, shoulders drooping, holding her drawing.
Joseph crouched. “The drawing competition?”
“The prize went to Arun. Mine was better.”
“You're disappointed.”
“Very.” She scuffed her shoe.
“That feels bad. You worked on that jungle all week.”
“Can we go home?”
“Yes. And shall we put your jungle on the wall?”
Ritu looked at her drawing. “…Okay. Next to the window.”
On the way home, she started humming again.

qa.q: What had Ritu drawn?
qa.a: A jungle.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as she came out with drooping shoulders?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and a bit resentful that she didn't win the prize.

qa.q: How did Joseph help Ritu handle the letdown?
qa.a: He named her disappointment, acknowledged her week of work and offered to put the drawing on the wall.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Ritu starts humming again?
qa.a: He is likely relieved and glad that her disappointment has passed.

grounding: A preschooler is disappointed at losing a prize, and her father names the feeling and lets it pass.

passage:
Sports day note, written by Reena, KG teacher.
Vikas came last in the running race. He walked off the track with his shoulders dropped and sat with his back to everyone. When I sat beside him, he said, “I'm always last.” I said, “You're disappointed. You really wanted to win.” He nodded and picked at the grass. I didn't try to cheer him up straight away. Ten minutes later he stood up and cheered loudly for his friend in the next race. The letdown passed.

qa.q: Where did Vikas come in the running race?
qa.a: Last.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he sat with his back to everyone?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and discouraged, believing he's always last.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Reena not to cheer Vikas up straight away?
qa.a: Letting the disappointment be named and pass on its own teaches him that letdowns are survivable.

qa.q: How might Vikas's friend feel hearing him cheer?
qa.a: The friend would likely feel supported and happy to have Vikas cheering.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler's disappointment after losing a race being named and allowed to pass.

passage: Goldie, the fish, was floating when Noor woke up. Jeevan, her father, told her simply: “Goldie died in the night. Her body stopped working. She won't swim again.” Noor was quiet all day, following him from room to room. At dinner she asked, “Will Goldie come back?” “No, sweetheart. But we can remember her.” That night, they buried Goldie in the balcony pot, and Noor drew a gold fish on a card. Jeevan kept bedtime the same: bath, story, song.

qa.q: Where did they bury Goldie?
qa.a: In the balcony pot.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling as she followed her father from room to room?
qa.a: She was sad and a bit unsettled after losing Goldie, and wanted to stay close to him.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan keep bedtime the same?
qa.a: A familiar routine helps a grieving child feel safe, alongside short, honest answers.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel answering Noor's question about Goldie?
qa.a: He likely feels tender and sad for her, but chooses to be honest and gentle.

grounding: A preschooler is quiet and clingy after her fish dies, and her father gives short honest answers and keeps the routine.

passage:
“Dadu, when are we going home?”
“This is our home now, Pema. In the city.”
“I mean real home. With the hills.”
Jagdish put down his newspaper. Pema had been quiet since the move, clinging to his kurta.
“You miss the hills.”
“And my friend. And our dog.”
“I miss them too. We live here now. But we can call your friend on Sunday.”
Pema leaned on him. “Can we have a dog here?”
“Let's think about it. Now, it's time for your bath, same as always.”

qa.q: When did Dadu say they could call Pema's friend?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as she clung to Dadu's kurta?
qa.a: She was sad and homesick for the hills, her friend and their dog.

qa.q: How did Jagdish support Pema without a long talk?
qa.a: He named her feeling, gave a short honest answer, offered a Sunday call and kept her routine with bath time.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when Pema says she misses the hills?
qa.a: He likely feels sad too, since he admits he misses them, but stays steady for her.

grounding: A preschooler shows sorrow after moving house, and her grandfather gives short honest explanations and keeps routine.

passage:
Note by Chaitanya, nursery teacher.
Suraj's dog died on the weekend. This week he has been quiet and clingy, staying close to me at play. Today he drew a brown dog with wings and asked, “Does it hurt to die?” I said, “No. When a body stops working, it doesn't feel pain anymore.” He nodded and coloured the wings. I kept his day the same as usual: circle, snack, sandpit. I've told his parents about the drawing and the question so they can talk at home.

qa.q: What did Suraj draw on the dog?
qa.a: Wings.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stayed close at play?
qa.a: He was sad and a little lost after his dog died, and staying close felt safer.

qa.q: Why was Chaitanya's short answer helpful?
qa.a: A short, honest answer met Suraj's real question without overwhelming him, and the usual routine kept him steady.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They'd likely feel grateful to know about his question and drawing, so they can support him at home.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler's sorrow in drawing and questions after his dog died, met with short honest answers and routine.

passage:
POP! The balloon burst next to Hafsa's ear. She shrieked and ran to Asif, grabbing his legs.
“Abbu! What was that?”
Asif crouched and held her. “You got a big fright. It was just the balloon. Look.” He picked up the red scrap.
“A balloon did that noise?”
“A balloon did that noise. You're safe.”
Hafsa touched the scrap carefully. “It's broken.”
“It is. Balloons pop sometimes, and it's loud, but it can't hurt you.”
Hafsa let go of his legs. “Can I blow up another?”

qa.q: What colour was the balloon scrap?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she shrieked and grabbed Asif's legs?
qa.a: She was alarmed and frightened by the sudden loud pop, not knowing what it was.

qa.q: How did Asif help Hafsa judge whether the danger was real?
qa.a: He reassured her quickly, showed her the popped balloon and explained that it was loud but couldn't hurt her.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Hafsa asks to blow up another?
qa.a: He likely feels relieved and amused that her fright passed so quickly.

grounding: A preschooler shrieks and runs to her father when a balloon pops, and his calm reassurance helps her judge the danger.

passage:
Note by Harish, preschool teacher.
During today's storm, the power went off with a loud click and the room went dark. Pradeep shrieked and ran to me, shouting, “A monster turned the lights off!” I held him and said calmly, “You got a fright. The storm made the power go off. There's no monster.” I switched on my torch and showed him the window with the rain. He stayed on my lap until the lights came back. He then said, “It was the storm, not a monster.”

qa.q: What did Pradeep think turned the lights off?
qa.a: A monster.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he shrieked and ran to Harish?
qa.a: He was alarmed and scared by the sudden dark and loud click, imagining a monster.

qa.q: How did Harish help Pradeep separate real from imagined danger?
qa.a: Harish reassured Pradeep quickly and showed him with a torch that the storm, not a monster, caused the dark.

qa.q: How might the other children feel seeing Harish stay calm?
qa.a: They'd likely feel calmer too, seeing an adult treat it as nothing dangerous.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler alarmed by a sudden power cut, and calm reassurance helping him tell real from imagined danger.

passage: The wedding procession came down the village lane with drums, and a firecracker exploded right near the gate. Ira screamed and ran to her mother, Yamini, burying her face in her lap. Yamini held her close. “That was a firecracker. It was very loud, but it's far now, and you're safe.” Ira peeked up. “Will it come here?” “No. It's in the lane, and the people with the crackers are careful.” Ira watched the dancing from Yamini's lap, hands ready over her ears.

qa.q: What exploded near the gate?
qa.a: A firecracker.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she ran and buried her face?
qa.a: She was alarmed and frightened by the sudden explosion near her.

qa.q: What did Yamini do that helped Ira judge the danger?
qa.a: She reassured her quickly, named what it was and explained it was far and handled carefully.

qa.q: What would change if Yamini had laughed at Ira's fright?
qa.a: Ira might feel embarrassed and more scared, instead of calming down enough to watch the dancing.

grounding: A preschooler runs to her mother when startled by a firecracker, and calm reassurance helps her judge the danger.

passage: In the KG classroom, Rafiq was doing a jigsaw puzzle of a train. Three pieces wouldn't fit. He growled, pushed the puzzle away and said, “I can't! It's stupid!” Charu Ma'am sat beside him. “You tried lots of pieces. That's hard work.” She pulled the puzzle back. “Let's just find the edges first. The straight ones.” Rafiq found one. Then another. “Now the red engine pieces.” Step by step, the train came together. Rafiq pressed in the last piece and shouted, “Done!”

qa.q: What was the jigsaw puzzle a picture of?
qa.a: A train.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he growled and pushed the puzzle away?
qa.a: He was frustrated and felt the puzzle was too hard, close to giving up.

qa.q: How did Charu Ma'am keep Rafiq from quitting?
qa.a: She praised his effort and broke the task into steps, edges first and then the red engine pieces.

qa.q: How might Charu Ma'am feel when Rafiq shouts “Done!”?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased and proud that he pushed through with her help.

grounding: A preschooler growls and gives up on a hard puzzle, and his teacher praises effort and breaks it into steps.

passage: I'm Nilesh, Vishal's big brother. Vishal was trying to tie his shoelaces on the step. He tried, got a knot, tried again, then kicked the shoe across the hall and yelled, “I hate laces!” Papa didn't tell him off. He sat next to him. “You've been trying a long time. That's frustrating.” Then he showed him just one step: “Make a bunny ear.” Vishal did. “Now another.” He did. I don't know if he'll remember tomorrow, but he tied one bow.

qa.q: What did Papa tell Vishal to make first?
qa.a: A bunny ear.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he kicked the shoe?
qa.a: He was frustrated after trying and failing many times, and angry at the laces.

passage:
Monday: Mohit tried to ride his new bicycle without stabilisers, fell twice, then kicked it and walked away. “I'll never ride it.” Neelam, his mother, said, “You tried hard.”
Wednesday: Neelam broke it into steps. “Today, just sit and push with your feet.” Mohit scooted along. “Now lift your feet for one second.” He did.
Saturday: Mohit pushed off, lifted his feet and pedalled five pushes before wobbling to a stop. “Mummy! I rode it!” Neelam cheered from the gate.

qa.q: How many pushes did Mohit pedal on Saturday?
qa.a: Five pushes.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling on Monday when he kicked the bicycle?
qa.a: He was frustrated and discouraged after falling twice, ready to give up.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: Neelam broke riding into small steps, first pushing with his feet, then lifting them for a second.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel on Saturday at the gate?
qa.a: She likely feels proud and delighted that Mohit kept going.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler's frustration with a bicycle is turned into progress by praising effort and breaking the task into steps.

passage:
Note by Jyoti, KG teacher.
Snack came late today because the van was delayed. By eleven, Himani was scowling and whining, and when her friend leaned on her, she pushed her away hard. Her friend cried. I didn't scold first. I noticed Himani's tiffin was still closed and she had skipped breakfast. I gave her a banana. Ten minutes later she was smiling, and she said sorry to her friend on her own. Hunger often looks like bad temper at this age.

qa.q: Why did snack come late?
qa.a: Because the van was delayed.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she pushed her friend away?
qa.a: She was irritated and cranky, most likely because she was hungry after skipping breakfast.

qa.q: How did Jyoti settle Himani's irritation?
qa.a: By noticing the hunger behind it and giving her a banana, rather than scolding first.

qa.q: How might Himani's friend feel when Himani says sorry?
qa.a: The friend would likely feel better and ready to play again.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler's irritation coming from hunger, settled by meeting the need.

passage: The bus back from the town market was packed and hot. Dhruv sat squashed between his sister Neelam and a big sack of onions. He whined, “Move!” and pushed Neelam's arm. She pushed back. “Stop it!” Then she saw his eyes drooping and his face flushed. It was past his nap time. Neelam sighed, lifted him onto her lap and let him lean on her shoulder. “Sleep. We'll wake you at our stop.” Within a minute he was snoring.

qa.q: What was Dhruv squashed between?
qa.a: His sister Neelam and a big sack of onions.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he whined and pushed Neelam?
qa.a: He was irritated and uncomfortable, tired and hot in the crowded bus.

qa.q: Which choice by Neelam worked, and why?
qa.a: She noticed he was tired and let him sleep on her lap, meeting the need behind his irritation.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when he starts snoring?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and a bit fond, glad the fighting is over.

grounding: A preschooler whines and pushes his sister on a crowded bus, and she sees tiredness behind it and lets him sleep.

passage: At the noisy birthday party in Edinburgh, music boomed and children shrieked. Omar scowled at everything. When his sister Freya tried to pull him into the dancing, he shoved her away. “Go away!” Freya was hurt. Their mother noticed Omar pressing his hands to his ears. She took him out to the quiet garden. “Too loud?” He nodded. They sat on the bench. After ten minutes, Omar went back in and said to Freya, “Sorry. It was too loud.” She took his hand, and they danced near the door.

qa.q: Where did their mother take Omar?
qa.a: Out to the quiet garden.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling when he shoved Freya away?
qa.a: He was irritated and overwhelmed by the loud music, which made him snappy.

qa.q: What did their mother do that settled Omar's irritation?
qa.a: She noticed his hands on his ears and took him somewhere quiet, meeting the need behind his mood.

qa.q: How did Freya feel when Omar shoved her?
qa.a: She was hurt, since she only wanted to dance with him.

grounding: A preschooler's irritation at a loud party is settled when his mother notices the noise and takes him somewhere quiet.
